h1: Working capital in a whisky business
title: Working Capital in a Whisky Business | Craft Beer School
desc: Where cash gets stuck in a whisky business: maturing stock, excise paid before sale, state receivables and packaging that cannot move.
teaser: A whisky business can be profitable on paper and short of cash in practice. Here is where the money goes while the spirit ages.
standfirst: Whisky ties up cash for longer than almost any consumer product. Spirit sits in casks for years, excise is often paid before the bottle sells and state-specific packaging cannot be moved across a border. This guide shows where working capital gets stuck and which levers actually move it.
sections:
Working capital is the cash tied up in running the business day to day: inventory plus money owed by customers, minus money owed to suppliers. A useful way to see it is the cash conversion cycle:

Cash conversion cycle = inventory days + receivable days - payable days

It measures how long a rupee spent on raw materials takes to come back as cash from a customer. A soft drinks company might turn that rupee around in weeks. A whisky company with aged products can take years. That single difference explains a lot about how distillers borrow, plan and price.
Maturing stock is the biggest lock on cash

Every litre of malt whisky laid down today will not be sold for at least three years if it is to be called Scotch. Older age statements take much longer. All the cost of making it, the cask and the warehouse space is paid now. The cash comes back only when it is sold.

Here is an illustrative cycle for a business heavy in aged whisky, using made-up round numbers. Inventory days of 400, receivable days of 60 and payable days of 45 give a cycle of 400 + 60 - 45 = 415 days. Change only the inventory days to 60, typical of a business selling mostly unaged blends. The cycle drops to 75 days. Same receivables, same suppliers, five times less cash locked up. Portfolio mix drives working capital more than any finance process does.

Most mainstream Indian whisky is a blend built on neutral spirit made from molasses or grain, with a share of malt whisky for flavour. Neutral spirit does not need years in wood. So the inventory days for a regular tier blend are far lower than for a single malt.

That is why the premium end of an Indian portfolio, single malts and aged blends, takes a share of working capital far larger than its share of volume. When a company moves its mix upwards, revenue per case rises. So does the cash tied up in stock. Our guide to the Indian whisky market explains the tiers.
Excise is often paid before the bottle sells

In India alcohol for human consumption is outside GST. Each state levies its own excise duty and fees. In many states the duty falls due when stock is released from the bonded warehouse or before it can be moved to the state's wholesale channel, not when a consumer buys the bottle. Duty can be a large multiple of the value of the liquid.

So a company may pay a large tax bill weeks or months before it sees the sales revenue. Some states also require deposits or bank guarantees for licences and permits. Rules and payment points vary by state and change, so finance teams work from the current notification for each state, not last year's.
Receivables depend on the state's route to market

Who owes you money depends on where you sell. In some states a government corporation is the only wholesaler. In others private distributors buy from the company. Payment terms and how reliably they are met differ by state and by year.

For a company selling in many states, receivable days are really a mix of very different arrangements. A national average can hide one state that is paying late. Analysts get more insight by breaking receivables down by state and channel than by tracking the total.
Packaging cannot always move across borders

Labels in India often carry state-specific details, including the maximum retail price and sometimes a statement that the bottle is for sale only in that state. Many states also require security holograms or excise labels of their own. So a pallet of finished stock or printed labels for one state cannot simply be shipped to another if demand shifts.

When a price change or a label rule change comes in, old labels can become scrap. Planning teams that order packaging in large runs to save cost per unit can end up with more cash stuck in packaging that may never be used.
The levers that actually move it

• Match fillings to realistic forecasts. Overfilling ties up cash for a decade. Our guide to forecasting with long lead times covers the method.
  • Plan releases around excise payment points. Moving stock out of bond only when it can be sold soon keeps duty from being paid early.
  • Watch the state mix. Growth in a state with slow payment changes cash needs even if volume growth looks healthy.
  • Cut slow SKUs. Every extra pack size or limited edition carries its own stock of glass, labels and finished goods.

A good first step is to rebuild your company's cash conversion cycle by product tier and by state. The averages will look tidy. The breakdown is where the decisions are.
faqs: Why does whisky need so much working capital?
Aged whisky is paid for years before it is sold. Excise is often paid before the bottle reaches a consumer. Both lock up cash for long periods.
Do Indian blends tie up as much cash as single malts?
No. Blends built on neutral spirit need little or no ageing, so their inventory days are much lower than those of aged malts.
Where should an analyst look first?
Break the cash conversion cycle down by product tier and by state. National averages hide the differences that drive cash needs.
